import Mathlib
/-! QED-M110: Logarithmically many conjugacy classes
Every finite group of order n splits into conjugacy classes. Is there one fixed constant c>0 such that every finite group of order n has at least c*log n conjugacy classes? The best known lower bounds lose a power of log log n, and the question is whether that loss is real.
Informal statement: Let $k(G)$ denote the number of conjugacy classes of a finite group $G$. Is $\inf\{k(G)/\log|G| : G \text{ finite}, |G|\ge 2\}>0$? Equivalently, either prove $k(G)\ge c\log|G|$ for an absolute $c>0$ and all finite $G$, or exhibit finite groups $G_i$ with $k(G_i)/\log|G_i|\to0$.
Formalization notes: `k(G)` is `Nat.card (ConjClasses G)` (Mathlib's quotient of `G` by
conjugacy). Groups range over `G : Type` with `[Group G] [Finite G]`; every finite group
is isomorphic to one in `Type` (e.g. on `Fin |G|`), and both `k(G)` and `|G|` are
isomorphism invariants, so this loses nothing. `Real.log` is the natural log; the base
only rescales `c`. The trivial group gives `log 1 = 0 ≤ k`, so including it is harmless
(matches `|G| ≥ 2` in the informal version). Claim: ∃ c > 0, ∀ finite G,
`c * log |G| ≤ k(G)`, i.e. the infimum is positive. ¬Claim is the existence, for every
c > 0, of a finite group with `k(G) < c log |G|`, i.e. a family with `k/log|G| → 0`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM110
noncomputable section

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] [Finite G],
    c * Real.log (Nat.card G : ℝ) ≤ (Nat.card (ConjClasses G) : ℝ)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM110

title: An APN permutation of GF(2^8)
credit: The 'big APN problem' (Dillon et al.; open since the 2009 n=6 discovery). Not named after a person.
premise_risks: Several 2026 sources are preprints, but the open status is long established in refereed literature.
Exhaustive search is infeasible (256! bijections), so a resolution needs ideas. A sufficiently clever structured search could still find an example.
The attribution of the even-dimension quadratic non-existence result was not re-verified in this round.
plain: A function f on the field with 256 elements is almost perfect nonlinear (APN) if, for every nonzero shift a, the difference f(x+a)+f(x) takes each value at most twice. APN bijections would be ideal S-boxes against differential attacks. In even dimension the only APN bijections known live on 64 elements (found in 2009). Does an APN bijection of GF(2^8) exist?
math: Does there exist a bijection $f:\mathbb F_{2^8}\to\mathbb F_{2^8}$ such that for all $a\in\mathbb F_{2^8}^{\times}$ and all $b\in\mathbb F_{2^8}$, $\#\{x\in\mathbb F_{2^8}: f(x+a)+f(x)=b\}\le 2$?
review_note: Known: There are no APN permutations for n=4 (Hou; exhaustive). Browning–Dillon–McQuistan–Wolfe 2010 found an APN permutation for n=6 (CCZ-equivalent to the Kim function). Hou, Nyberg and others showed that power (monomial) APN permutations do not exist in even dimension. Classical results (attributed to Nyberg / Seberry–Zhang–Zheng; I did not re-verify the source here) exclude quadratic APN permutations in even dimension. Millions of quadratic APN functions in dimension 8 are known (arXiv 2508.04644; ePrint 2026/2799), none CCZ-equivalent to a permutation as far as tested. arXiv 2611.10269 and ePrint 2026/2800 rule out the family $x^3+a^{-1}\mathrm{Tr}(a^3x^9)$ for all even $n\le24$. Recent papers treat existence for even $n\ge8$ as open.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M111: An APN permutation of GF(2^8)
A function f on the field with 256 elements is almost perfect nonlinear (APN) if, for every nonzero shift a, the difference f(x+a)+f(x) takes each value at most twice. APN bijections would be ideal S-boxes against differential attacks. In even dimension the only APN bijections known live on 64 elements (found in 2009). Does an APN bijection of GF(2^8) exist?
Informal statement: Does there exist a bijection $f:\mathbb F_{2^8}\to\mathbb F_{2^8}$ such that for all $a\in\mathbb F_{2^8}^{\times}$ and all $b\in\mathbb F_{2^8}$, $\#\{x\in\mathbb F_{2^8}: f(x+a)+f(x)=b\}\le 2$?
Formalization notes: `𝔽_{2^8}` is Mathlib's `GaloisField 2 8` (the splitting field of
`X^(2^8) - X` over `ZMod 2`, a field with exactly 256 elements, unique up to isomorphism;
`Fact (Nat.Prime 2)` is a global instance). Only its additive group (≅ (ZMod 2)^8) is
actually used, so the choice of model is immaterial. A bijection is an
`Equiv`. The count `#{x | f(x+a) + f(x) = b}` is `Set.ncard` of a subset of a finite
type, hence the true cardinality. In characteristic 2, `+` equals `-`, matching the usual
derivative `f(x+a) - f(x)`. Claim is the existence statement; ¬Claim says no APN
permutation of `GF(2^8)` exists. Either is a resolution.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM111
noncomputable section

/-- `f` is almost perfect nonlinear on `GF(2^8)`. -/
def IsAPN (f : GaloisField 2 8 → GaloisField 2 8) : Prop :=
  ∀ a : GaloisField 2 8, a ≠ 0 → ∀ b : GaloisField 2 8,
    {x : GaloisField 2 8 | f (x + a) + f x = b}.ncard ≤ 2

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ f : GaloisField 2 8 ≃ GaloisField 2 8, IsAPN f

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM111

title: Word problem for one-relation monoids
credit: S. I. Adian (posed c. 1960); reduction by Adian and G. U. Oganesyan
premise_risks: the precise form of the Adian-Oganesyan reduction (bUa=a) was taken from secondary knowledge of the survey, not verified from the full text in this check
famous within combinatorial semigroup theory; vetter should judge 'famous problem in disguise' (it is stated directly, not disguised)
plain: Take a monoid with a single defining relation u = v between two words. Is its word problem always decidable: for each such monoid, is there an algorithm that, given two words, decides whether they are equal in it? This is open even though the corresponding question for one-relator groups was settled long ago.
math: For a finite alphabet $A$ and $u,v\in A^*$, let $\equiv_{u,v}$ be the smallest congruence on $A^*$ containing $(u,v)$. Problem: does every one-relation monoid $\mathrm{Mon}\langle A\mid u=v\rangle$ have decidable word problem, i.e. is $\{(w_1,w_2): w_1\equiv_{u,v}w_2\}$ decidable for every fixed $A,u,v$? Board Claim: yes. (Uniform variant: the set of all $(A,u,v,w_1,w_2)$ with $w_1\equiv_{u,v}w_2$ is decidable. By Adian--Oganesyan (1978; two-generator form 1987) it suffices to treat $\mathrm{Mon}\langle a,b\mid bUa=aVa\rangle$ and $\mathrm{Mon}\langle a,b\mid bUa=a\rangle$, $U,V\in\{a,b\}^*$; both cases remain open. Undecidability for one fixed such monoid settles the problem negatively.)
review_note: Known: Decidable for special monoids <A|r=1> (Adian 1960; Makanin's reduction to the group of units), for Adian's left- or right-cycle-free presentations (u and v differ in first letter, or in last letter), and many subcases (Adian-Oganesyan 1987, Lallement 1974, Kobayashi, and Nyberg-Brodda's monadic results). Adian-Oganesyan reduced the general problem to <a,b | bUa = a>. Surveys: Nyberg-Brodda, 'The word problem for one-relation monoids: a survey', Semigroup Forum 103 (2021), arXiv:2105.02853. Related undecidability: one-relator inverse monoids (R. D. Gray, Invent. Math. 2020). Status reconfirmed open in Gray-Steinberg arXiv:2507.04819 (v2 March 2026) and Foniqi-Gray-Nyberg-Brodda (Canad. J. Math. 2024, arXiv:2305.15672), where the related prefix-membership problem is shown undecidable for some positive one-relator groups.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M112: Word problem for one-relation monoids
Take a finite alphabet and two words u and v, and declare u = v. Two words are then equal in the monoid if you can turn one into the other by repeatedly swapping a copy of u for v, or v for u, somewhere inside the word. Magnus showed in 1932 that groups with one relation always have a solvable word problem. Is there an algorithm that, given u, v and two more words, decides whether those two words are equal in this monoid?
Informal statement: For a finite alphabet $A$ and $u,v\in A^*$, let $\equiv_{u,v}$ be the smallest congruence on $A^*$ containing $(u,v)$. Does every one-relation monoid $\mathrm{Mon}\langle A\mid u=v\rangle$ have decidable word problem, i.e. is $\{(w_1,w_2): w_1\equiv_{u,v}w_2\}$ decidable for every fixed $A,u,v$? Board Claim: yes.
Formalization notes:
* Words are `List ℕ` (letters are natural numbers). For FIXED `u, v`, the predicate below is the
  word problem of `⟨ℕ | u = v⟩`. Letters not occurring in `u`, `v` are inert: no rewriting step
  creates, destroys or moves them, and every occurrence of `u` (also the empty word) sits inside one
  maximal inert-free segment. Hence `w₁ ≡ w₂` iff the two words have the same sequence of inert
  letters and corresponding segments are equivalent in `⟨A | u = v⟩`, `A` = letters of `u, v`.
  So this word problem is decidable iff that of `⟨A | u = v⟩` is (for any finite `A ⊇` letters of
  `u, v`: restriction gives one direction, segment splitting the other). Quantifying over all
  `u v : List ℕ` covers every finite alphabet up to renaming letters.
* `OneStep u v x y` : `y` is obtained from `x` by replacing one occurrence of `u` by `v`.
  `Relation.EqvGen (OneStep u v)` is exactly the congruence generated by `(u, v)` on the free
  monoid (the closure is compatible with concatenation; every congruence containing `(u,v)`
  contains each step). Empty `u` or `v` is allowed (special monoids `⟨A | r = 1⟩`).
* `Claim` (the board claim, NON-uniform): for every fixed `u, v`, the set of pairs `(w₁, w₂)` with
  `w₁ ≡_{u,v} w₂` is computable (Mathlib's `ComputablePred` on `List ℕ × List ℕ`). This is a
  genuine computability statement about each fixed set, not a classical triviality.
  `¬Claim` = some one-relation monoid has undecidable word problem.
* `ClaimUniform` (stronger variant, for reference only): one algorithm for all `(u, v, w₁, w₂)`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM112
noncomputable section

/-- One rewriting step with the relation `u = v`: replace one occurrence of `u` by `v`. -/
def OneStep (u v : List ℕ) (x y : List ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ a b : List ℕ, x = a ++ u ++ b ∧ y = a ++ v ++ b

/-- `w₁ ≡ w₂` in the monoid `⟨ℕ | u = v⟩`: the congruence generated by `(u, v)`, i.e. the
equivalence closure of single rewriting steps. -/
def OneRelEquiv (u v w₁ w₂ : List ℕ) : Prop :=
  Relation.EqvGen (OneStep u v) w₁ w₂

/-- Every one-relation monoid has decidable word problem. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ u v : List ℕ, ComputablePred (fun p : List ℕ × List ℕ => OneRelEquiv u v p.1 p.2)

/-- Uniform variant (stronger; not the board claim). -/
def ClaimUniform : Prop :=
  ComputablePred (fun p : List ℕ × List ℕ × List ℕ × List ℕ =>
    OneRelEquiv p.1 p.2.1 p.2.2.1 p.2.2.2)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM112

title: Big line or six visible points
credit: J. Kara, A. Por, D. R. Wood (2005); row clique=6 framed after Abel et al. 2011 and Bonnet/Cambie 2026
premise_risks: very active area in 2026 (four unrefereed preprints); could be resolved soon
the l=4 results it builds on are unrefereed 2026 preprints, though the Claim itself does not depend on them
plain: Two points of a finite set in the plane see each other if the segment between them passes through no other point of the set. Prove that for every l there is an N such that any N points in the plane contain either l points on a line or 6 points that all see each other. This is known for 5 points that all see each other (for every l), and since 2026 for 6 such points when l = 4.
math: For finite $P\subset\mathbb R^2$, call $p,q\in P$ visible if $[p,q]\cap P=\{p,q\}$. Claim: for every $\ell\ge 3$ there is $N(\ell)$ such that every $P\subset\mathbb R^2$ with $|P|\ge N(\ell)$ contains $\ell$ collinear points or $6$ pairwise visible points.
review_note: Known: Clique <=4, every l: Kara-Por-Wood (Discrete Comput. Geom. 2005). Clique 5, line 4: Addario-Berry et al.; clique 5, every l: Abel, Ballinger, Bose, Collette, Dujmovic, Hurtado, Kominers, Langerman, Por, Wood, Graphs Combin. 27 (2011). Clique 6, line 4: Bonnet arXiv:2608.19468 (N ~ 10^11055931), improved to N<=880 by Cambie arXiv:2609.21035 (v2 Nov 2026). Bhattacharya-Das-Islam-Mohapatra-Sen arXiv:2609.25727: no 4 collinear forces 7 points missing at most one visibility. Structured regimes (points on a cubic, few ordinary lines, irreducible curves): Sarkar arXiv:2605.00918. All other (line, clique) pairs with clique>=6 open, per Bonnet's introduction.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M113: Big line or six visible points
Two points of a finite set in the plane see each other if the segment between them passes through no other point of the set. Prove that for every l there is an N such that any N points in the plane contain either l points on a line or 6 points that all see each other. This is known for 5 points that all see each other (for every l), and since 2026 for 6 such points when l = 4.
Informal statement: For finite $P\subset\mathbb R^2$, call $p,q\in P$ visible if $[p,q]\cap P=\{p,q\}$. Claim: for every $\ell\ge 3$ there is $N(\ell)$ such that every $P\subset\mathbb R^2$ with $|P|\ge N(\ell)$ contains $\ell$ collinear points or $6$ pairwise visible points.
Formalization notes:
* The plane is `ℝ × ℝ` (an affine space over itself); collinearity (`Collinear ℝ`) and closed
  segments (`segment ℝ p q`) are affine notions, so no Euclidean structure is needed.
* `Visible P p q` : every point of `P` on the closed segment `[p, q]` is an endpoint. For `p = q`
  this holds trivially; it only matters for distinct points of the 6-set `C`, which has 6 distinct
  elements because `C.card = 6`.
* "Contains `ℓ` collinear points": a subset `L ⊆ P` with `|L| = ℓ` that is collinear (equivalent to
  "at least `ℓ`", by taking subsets). "6 pairwise visible points": `C ⊆ P`, `|C| = 6`, all pairs
  visible with respect to the whole set `P` (not just `C`), as in the big-line-big-clique conjecture.
* `Claim` = the clique-6 row of the big-line-big-clique conjecture for every line size `ℓ ≥ 3`.
  `¬Claim` = some `ℓ` and arbitrarily large point sets with no `ℓ` collinear and no 6 mutually
  visible points. The hypothesis `3 ≤ ℓ` only excludes trivial cases (for `ℓ ≤ 2` any 2 points are
  collinear).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM113
noncomputable section

/-- `p` and `q` see each other in `P`: no point of `P` other than `p`, `q` lies on `[p, q]`. -/
def Visible (P : Finset (ℝ × ℝ)) (p q : ℝ × ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ r ∈ P, r ∈ segment ℝ p q → r = p ∨ r = q

/-- Every sufficiently large finite planar set has `ℓ` collinear points or 6 pairwise visible points. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ℓ : ℕ, 3 ≤ ℓ → ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ P : Finset (ℝ × ℝ), N ≤ P.card →
    (∃ L : Finset (ℝ × ℝ), L ⊆ P ∧ L.card = ℓ ∧ Collinear ℝ (L : Set (ℝ × ℝ))) ∨
    (∃ C : Finset (ℝ × ℝ), C ⊆ P ∧ C.card = 6 ∧ ∀ p ∈ C, ∀ q ∈ C, Visible P p q)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM113

title: Is there an aperiodic polyomino?
credit: Open problem as posed in A. Winslow, 'Some open problems in polyomino tilings' (DLT 2018); long-standing folklore (Golomb)
premise_risks: 'Polyomino' may be required to be simply connected in some sources; the Claim allows holes, which only makes the existence claim easier, so the vetter may prefer the simply connected version
existence proofs would likely be computer-assisted substitution arguments, heavy but finite in Lean
related to existing board items on hat/spectre tilings (M056, M057, N-117) but about a different tile class
plain: A polyomino is a shape made of unit squares glued edge to edge with no holes. In 2023 a single tile was found that tiles the plane only non-periodically, but it is built from kites, not squares. Is there a polyomino that tiles the plane (rotations and reflections allowed) but has no tiling that a translation maps onto itself?
math: A polyomino is a finite $P\subset\mathbb Z^2$ such that the union of the closed unit squares $c+[0,1]^2$, $c\in P$, is a closed topological disk. A tiling by $P$ is a set $\mathcal T$ of tiles $g(P)$, with $g(x)=Ax+b$, $A\in D_4\subset GL_2(\mathbb Z)$ and $b\in\mathbb Z^2$, that partition $\mathbb Z^2$. $P$ is aperiodic if some tiling exists but no tiling satisfies $\mathcal T+v=\mathcal T$ for any $v\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$. Problem: does an aperiodic polyomino exist? Board Claim: yes. A proof that every polyomino that tiles also has a periodic tiling settles the problem negatively. (Variant: allow holes, i.e. require only that $P$ is edge-connected.)
review_note: Known: Translations only: a polyomino tiles iff it tiles isohedrally/periodically (Wijshoff-van Leeuwen 1984; Beauquier-Nivat 1991). k-anisohedral polyominoes known for k<=6 (Winslow survey, Open Problem 6 asks for k>=7). Aperiodic sets of 3 polyominoes (with isometries) known; aperiodic sets of 2 polyominoes unknown (Winslow, Open Problem 8); translational aperiodic sets of 7 polyominoes (Yang-Zhang arXiv:2412.17382). Undecidability for sets of 5 polyominoes (Ollinger 2009). Non-polyomino aperiodic monotiles: hat and spectre (Smith-Myers-Kaplan-Goodman-Strauss 2023/24, Combinatorial Theory). Survey: A. Winslow, 'Some open problems in polyomino tilings', DLT 2018.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M114: Is there an aperiodic polyomino?
A polyomino is a shape made of unit squares glued edge to edge with no holes. In 2023 a single tile was found that tiles the plane only non-periodically, but it is built from kites, not squares. Is there a polyomino that tiles the plane (rotations and reflections allowed) but has no tiling that a translation maps onto itself?
Informal statement: A polyomino is a finite $P\subset\mathbb Z^2$ such that the union of the closed unit squares $c+[0,1]^2$, $c\in P$, is a closed topological disk. A tiling by $P$ is a set $\mathcal T$ of tiles $g(P)$, with $g(x)=Ax+b$, $A\in D_4\subset GL_2(\mathbb Z)$ and $b\in\mathbb Z^2$, that partition $\mathbb Z^2$. $P$ is aperiodic if some tiling exists but no tiling satisfies $\mathcal T+v=\mathcal T$ for any $v\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$. Board Claim: an aperiodic polyomino exists.
Formalization notes:
* Cells are `ℤ × ℤ` (cell `c` is the closed square `c + [0,1]²`). Two cells are 4-adjacent
  (`Adj4`) if they share an edge (`|Δx| + |Δy| = 1`). `Conn4 S`: any two cells of `S` are joined by
  a path of 4-adjacent cells inside `S`.
* Polyomino (`IsPolyomino`): `P` finite (a `Finset`), nonempty, `P` 4-connected, and the complement
  `ℤ² \ P` 4-connected. This is the standard combinatorial characterization of "the union of the
  squares is a closed topological disk": if both are 4-connected then there are no holes (a bounded
  complement component would be a separate 4-component) and no pinch points (two diagonal cells of
  `P` whose other two neighbours at that corner are outside `P`: a 4-path in `P` joining the two
  diagonal cells closes up, with the diagonal, into an 8-connected closed curve of cells, which
  encloses one of the two outside corner cells and so cuts it off from the infinite complement,
  since 4-paths cannot cross 8-closed curves). Without holes or pinches the union is a compact
  connected 2-manifold with boundary in the plane with connected complement, hence a disk; the
  converse is immediate. (Using a homeomorphism to the closed disk directly would make
  any existence proof require a Schoenflies-type argument for the specific tile, so the
  combinatorial form is used.)
* `D₄` is enumerated as `Bool × Bool × Bool`: optionally swap coordinates, then optionally negate
  each coordinate. These are exactly the 8 signed permutation matrices, i.e. the full dihedral
  group `D₄ ⊂ GL₂(ℤ)` of the square lattice. Placed copy: `place P g b = {d4 g c + b | c ∈ P}`.
  (Applying `A` to cell labels rather than to squares just reindexes the cells of the image
  square set by a fixed lattice translation, which is absorbed into `b`.)
* A tiling is a SET of placed copies (sets of cells), not a family of placements, so a tile with
  symmetries is not counted twice; every cell lies in exactly one tile. Tiling `ℤ²` by cells is the
  same as tiling the plane by the closed unit squares (with interiors disjoint).
* Periodic: `T + v = T` for some `v ≠ 0` (translation of the set of tiles). `Aperiodic P`: some
  tiling exists and no tiling has any nonzero period (as in the informal statement). For a single
  tile in `ℤ²` (a 2D shift of finite type) this coincides with "no doubly periodic tiling", since
  a tiling with one period yields a doubly periodic one.
* `Claim` = an aperiodic polyomino exists. `¬Claim` = every polyomino that tiles the plane with
  rotations/reflections also admits a tiling with a nonzero translational period. Neither is
  vacuous: `IsTiling` is satisfiable (e.g. the monomino) and forces all tiles to be copies of `P`.
  The variant allowing holes (dropping the complement condition) is not encoded.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM114
noncomputable section

/-- Edge adjacency of cells. -/
def Adj4 (a b : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := |a.1 - b.1| + |a.2 - b.2| = 1

/-- `S` is 4-connected: any two of its cells are joined by an edge-adjacent path inside `S`. -/
def Conn4 (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  ∀ a ∈ S, ∀ b ∈ S,
    Relation.ReflTransGen (fun x y : ℤ × ℤ => x ∈ S ∧ y ∈ S ∧ Adj4 x y) a b

/-- Polyomino (simply connected): nonempty, 4-connected, with 4-connected complement. -/
def IsPolyomino (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  P.Nonempty ∧ Conn4 (P : Set (ℤ × ℤ)) ∧ Conn4 ((P : Set (ℤ × ℤ))ᶜ)

/-- The 8 elements of `D₄ ⊂ GL₂(ℤ)`: optional coordinate swap, then optional sign changes. -/
def d4 (g : Bool × Bool × Bool) (c : ℤ × ℤ) : ℤ × ℤ :=
  let s : ℤ × ℤ := if g.1 then (c.2, c.1) else c
  ((if g.2.1 then -s.1 else s.1), (if g.2.2 then -s.2 else s.2))

/-- The copy `g(P) + b` of `P`. -/
def place (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) (g : Bool × Bool × Bool) (b : ℤ × ℤ) : Set (ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {z : ℤ × ℤ | ∃ c ∈ P, z = d4 g c + b}

/-- `T` is a tiling of `ℤ²` by isometric copies of `P`. -/
def IsTiling (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) (T : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ))) : Prop :=
  (∀ t ∈ T, ∃ g : Bool × Bool × Bool, ∃ b : ℤ × ℤ, t = place P g b) ∧
    ∀ z : ℤ × ℤ, ∃! t : Set (ℤ × ℤ), t ∈ T ∧ z ∈ t

/-- Translate every tile of `T` by `v`. -/
def translateTiling (v : ℤ × ℤ) (T : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ))) : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ)) :=
  {t : Set (ℤ × ℤ) | ∃ s ∈ T, t = (fun z : ℤ × ℤ => z + v) '' s}

/-- `P` tiles, but no tiling by `P` has a nonzero translational period. -/
def Aperiodic (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  (∃ T : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ)), IsTiling P T) ∧
    ∀ T : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ)), IsTiling P T → ∀ v : ℤ × ℤ, v ≠ 0 → translateTiling v T ≠ T

/-- There exists an aperiodic (simply connected) polyomino. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ), IsPolyomino P ∧ Aperiodic P

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM114

title: Returning to the identity in SL(3,Z)
credit: Open problem as recorded by I. Potapov and coauthors and in R. Dong's survey (2023)
premise_risks: Lean decidability statement via ComputablePred on lists of Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℤ is easy to state; undecidability would need Turing-reduction infrastructure
plain: You are given finitely many 3x3 integer matrices with determinant 1. Can some nonempty product of them (in any order, with repetition) equal the identity matrix? For 2x2 matrices there is an algorithm, and for 4x4 matrices it is known that none exists. Decide whether an algorithm exists for 3x3.
math: Let $\mathcal I_3=\{(M_1,\dots,M_k): k\ge1,\ M_i\in SL(3,\mathbb Z),\ \exists\, m\ge1,\ i_1,\dots,i_m\in\{1,\dots,k\}:\ M_{i_1}\cdots M_{i_m}=I_3\}$, with instances given as finite lists of integer matrices. Problem: is $\mathcal I_3$ decidable? Board Claim: $\mathcal I_3$ is decidable. A proof of undecidability settles the problem negatively.
review_note: Known: SL(2,Z): identity and membership decidable (Choffrut-Karhumaki 2005; Bell-Potapov; Potapov-Semukhin for nonsingular 2x2 integer matrices, SODA 2017). 3x3: mortality (zero matrix) undecidable for Z^{3x3} (Paterson 1970), but the identity problem is not covered. SL(4,Z): identity problem undecidable (Bell-Potapov 2010, via F2 x F2). Identity problem decidable for the Heisenberg group H(3,Z) (Ko-Niskanen-Potapov, ICALP 2018, arXiv:1706.04166), for SA(2,Z) (Dong, arXiv:2301.09502), and for 4x4 unitriangular matrices (arXiv:2202.05225). Survey: R. Dong, 'Recent advances in algorithmic problems for semigroups', arXiv:2309.10943 (ACM SIGLOG News 2023): status of all listed problems open for SL(3,Z).
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M115: Returning to the identity in SL(3,Z)
You are given finitely many 3x3 integer matrices with determinant 1. Can some nonempty product of them (in any order, with repetition) equal the identity matrix? For 2x2 matrices there is an algorithm, and for 4x4 matrices it is known that none exists. Decide whether an algorithm exists for 3x3.
Informal statement: Let $\mathcal I_3=\{(M_1,\dots,M_k): k\ge1,\ M_i\in SL(3,\mathbb Z),\ \exists\, m\ge1,\ i_1,\dots,i_m\in\{1,\dots,k\}:\ M_{i_1}\cdots M_{i_m}=I_3\}$, with instances given as finite lists of integer matrices. Is $\mathcal I_3$ decidable? Board Claim: $\mathcal I_3$ is decidable.
Formalization notes:
* Instances are `List (Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ)`: a list of 3×3 arrays of natural numbers, each entry
  decoded to an integer by the zig-zag bijection `zz : ℕ → ℤ` (`2n ↦ n`, `2n+1 ↦ -(n+1)`). This is a
  computable bijection, so it is just a `Primcodable` encoding of lists of integer matrices (it
  avoids relying on a `Primcodable ℤ` / `Matrix` instance). `toMat` turns an array into a
  `Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℤ`.
* `Ident3 L`: every matrix in `L` has determinant 1 (membership in `SL(3,ℤ)`), and some NONEMPTY
  word `w` in the indices of `L` (repetition allowed, any order) has product `1`. The empty list
  is automatically a no-instance (`Fin 0` admits no nonempty word), matching `k ≥ 1`. Lists
  containing a matrix of determinant `≠ 1` are no-instances; since the determinant test is
  computable this does not change decidability (it is the language $\mathcal I_3$ literally).
* `List.prod` multiplies left to right, `M_{i_1} ⋯ M_{i_m}`; the order convention is irrelevant
  for the identity problem anyway (reverse words).
* Decidability is Mathlib's `ComputablePred`. `Claim` = the identity problem for `SL(3,ℤ)` is
  decidable; `¬Claim` = it is undecidable. The predicate is r.e. (enumerate words), so the content
  is co-r.e.-ness / an algorithm; neither side is trivial.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM115
noncomputable section

/-- Zig-zag bijection `ℕ → ℤ`: `2n ↦ n`, `2n+1 ↦ -(n+1)`. -/
def zz (n : ℕ) : ℤ :=
  if n % 2 = 0 then ((n / 2 : ℕ) : ℤ) else -((n / 2 : ℕ) : ℤ) - 1

/-- The integer matrix encoded by a 3×3 array of codes. -/
def toMat (A : Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ) : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℤ :=
  Matrix.of (fun i j : Fin 3 => zz (A i j))

/-- `L` is a list of `SL(3,ℤ)` matrices some nonempty product of which is the identity. -/
def Ident3 (L : List (Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ)) : Prop :=
  (∀ A ∈ L, (toMat A).det = 1) ∧
    ∃ w : List (Fin L.length), w ≠ [] ∧
      (w.map (fun i : Fin L.length => toMat (L.get i))).prod = 1

/-- The identity problem for `SL(3,ℤ)` is decidable. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ComputablePred Ident3

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM115
